**CHAPTER I**  
**CAPSTONE PROJECT BACKGROUND**

#  **INTRODUCTION**

**1.1 Project Context** 

           CodiSmile Dental Clinic currently relies on manual visual examination and professional judgment to identify dental caries and other visible dental conditions from patient examinations and intraoral images. Although this approach is essential to dental practice, manually reviewing images may be time-consuming and can result in variations in assessment and documentation. To support the existing process, the proponents propose Toothwise: Teeth Cavity Detection with Recommendation System Using YOLOv12 for CodiSmile Dental Clinic , an AI-assisted system that analyzes intraoral images and detects possible dental conditions using the YOLOv12 object detection model. The system provides visual detection results, condition labels, descriptions, and preventive recommendations to assist dentists and improve patient understanding. Toothwise is intended to serve as a supplementary screening and documentation tool, while final interpretation and clinical decisions remain the responsibility of licensed dental professionals.

Dental caries, commonly referred to as tooth decay or cavities, remains one of the most prevalent non-communicable health conditions in the world. The World Health Organization (2024) estimates that oral diseases affect nearly 3.7 billion people globally, with untreated dental caries in permanent teeth identified as the single most widespread health condition based on Global Burden of Disease 2021 data. Despite its prevalence, a significant portion of the population, particularly those in geographically isolated or economically disadvantaged communities, continues to face substantial barriers in accessing timely and adequate dental care. The financial cost of consultations, the distance to dental facilities, and low oral health literacy frequently result in delayed care-seeking, by which point cavities have often advanced beyond their most treatable stages. According to Qari et al. (2023), untreated dental caries does not just cause physical pain, it also affects a person's confidence and overall quality of life.

A critical dimension of the current dental care challenge lies in the inconsistency of manual cavity screening practices. The Journal of Evidence-Based Dental Practice (2025) noted that clinical examination outcomes frequently vary depending on the examiner, as different dental practitioners may arrive at differing findings when assessing the same patient for carious lesions. This inter-examiner variability is particularly problematic in high-volume clinic settings where practitioner fatigue and time pressure can further compromise screening reliability. Research has shown that deep learning models are capable of detecting dental cavities with accuracy that is on par with, or sometimes even better than, trained clinicians, as confirmed by systematic reviews from Schwendicke et al. (2021) and Mohammad Rahimi et al. (2022). This makes AI a genuinely useful tool for supplementing human judgment during screenings.

Intraoral cameras have also changed the way dentists work. Instead of relying purely on what they can see with a mirror and a light, dentists can now capture clear, detailed images of the inside of the mouth. Studies like the one by Kang et al. (2024) show that these images are more than good enough to serve as input for AI-based cavity detection systems, producing consistent and reliable results during actual clinical use. It is this imaging modality that serves as the primary data source for Toothwise during patient screenings at CodiSmile Dental Clinic.

The AI model powering this system is YOLOv12, which was introduced by Tian et al. (2025) as an attention-centric object detection framework. Compared to previous versions in the YOLO family, YOLOv12 uses area attention mechanisms that help it focus selectively on spatially relevant regions, something that happens regularly in dental images where carious lesions appear as small, low-contrast areas across multiple tooth surfaces simultaneously. Its combination of speed and accuracy makes it practical for real-time use during clinical consultations.

This project was created in partnership with CodiSmile Dental Clinic, which serves as the deployment site and clinical reference point throughout the study. The goal is not to take the place of the dentist but to give them a more efficient and objective tool to work with. With Toothwise integrated into the clinic's workflow, cavity screenings can be done faster, findings can be documented more consistently, and patients can walk away with a clearer understanding of their oral health through the system's personalized prevention plan feature. 

# **1.2  Problem Statement**

The following problem statements identify the core challenges that this study seeks to address in relation to dental screening accuracy, real-time AI detection, and accessible preventive care at CodiSmile Dental Clinic:  
   
1\.  	What challenges are encountered in the current manual dental screening process at CodiSmile Dental Clinic that lead to missed dental conditions, including caries, calculus accumulation, tooth discoloration, and gingival abnormalities, due to human error and inconsistent visual assessment methods?  
2\.  	How can a YOLOv12-based deep learning model be trained and optimized to perform accurate, automated, multi-condition detection of dental anomalies from patient-submitted intraoral images with high precision and reliability?  
3\.  	How can Toothwise be designed to present AI-generated detection results, including bounding box annotations, condition labels, and plain-language descriptions in a format that enables licensed dentists at CodiSmile Dental Clinic to efficiently interpret and act on screening findings?  
4\.  	What recommendation plan can be generated by Toothwise to improve the dental health of the patient based on AI-detected findings?  
5\.  	How do the respondents evaluate the performance of the Toothwise in terms of functional suitability and other relevant software quality dimensions?

 **1.3  Objective of the Study**

# **General Objective**

 	This study will develop Tooth Wise, a teeth detection with Recommendation System that integrates a YOLOv12-based real-time cavity detection model with an intraoral camera and a personalized prevention plan generator, to provide accurate, accessible, and automated dental screening support for licensed dentists and patients at CodiSmile Dental Clinic.  
Furthermore, the study evaluates the developed software artifact against the international software quality standards defined in the ISO/IEC 25010 Software Product Quality Model, ensuring that the system fulfills rigorous benchmarks for technical robustness, clinical utility, operational safety, and overall user acceptability within the active practice environment of CodiSmile Dental Clinic.

# **Specific Objectives**

1. To develop and implement an AI-assisted dental screening system using YOLOv12 that addresses the challenges of human error and inconsistency in manual dental screening, delivering objective and reliable detection results during consultations at CodiSmile Dental Clinic.  
2. To train and evaluate a YOLOv12 deep learning model using annotated dental image datasets to accurately detect and classify dental caries and periodontal anomalies from live intraoral camera footage in real time.  
3. To develop an AI-generated detection system through bounding boxes, labels, and plain language descriptions, enabling CodiSmile dentists to efficiently interpret and act on screening results.  
4. To build a personalized prevention plan feature that translates AI-detected dental findings into clear, actionable, and patient-friendly oral health guidance, promoting early intervention and improved dental health awareness among patients of CodiSmile Dental Clinic.  
5. To evaluate the software performance, quality, and acceptability of the Toothwise system using a standardized evaluation instrument grounded in the ISO/IEC 25010 Software Product Quality Model, gathering quantitative and qualitative evaluations from IT professionals and dental clinical practitioners across eight product quality dimensions: Functional Suitability, Performance Efficiency, Compatibility, Usability, Reliability, Security, Maintainability, and Portability.

### **1.3.1 ISO/IEC 25010 Software Product Quality Framework**

The evaluation of Toothwise is anchored on the ISO/IEC 25010 Software Product Quality Model, an internationally recognized software engineering standard governed by the Systems and Software Quality Requirements and Evaluation (SQuaRE) series. ISO/IEC 25010 supersedes the earlier ISO/IEC 9126 standard, establishing a comprehensive taxonomy of eight (8) quality characteristics and sub-characteristics essential for verifying clinical software systems:

1. **Functional Suitability.** Evaluates the degree to which Toothwise meets specified clinical screening requirements when operated under defined conditions. This encompasses *Functional Completeness* (full integration of patient records, intraoral image capture/upload, multi-class YOLOv8/v12 cavity and gum inflammation detection, KNN prevention plan recommendation, clinical notes, and PDF reporting), *Functional Correctness* (precision and recall of detected bounding boxes and 0–100 risk scoring), and *Functional Appropriateness* (workflow alignment with dental consultation procedures).
2. **Performance Efficiency.** Assesses the performance of Toothwise relative to the resources consumed. This includes *Time Behavior* (sub-second AI inference times, with YOLOv12 achieving rapid attention-centric inference and low API response latencies), *Resource Utilization* (efficient local server CPU/GPU footprint and connection pooling), and *Capacity* (robust PostgreSQL database performance supporting hundreds of simultaneous screening records and high-resolution images).
3. **Compatibility.** Measures the capability of Toothwise to function concurrently with other clinic applications. This encompasses *Co-existence* (running reliably in local server and workstation operating environments alongside clinic management utilities) and *Interoperability* (seamless JSON-based data exchange across frontend, backend, and intraoral camera USB video interfaces).
4. **Usability.** Examines the effectiveness, efficiency, and user satisfaction of the system interface. Sub-characteristics include *Appropriateness Recognizability* (immediate visual clarity of risk badges and bounding boxes), *Learnability* (intuitive navigation for dental staff and patients), *Operability* (ergonomic capture and review controls), *User Error Protection* (Pydantic schema validation, confirmation modals, and boundary enforcement), *User Interface Aesthetics* (clean, professional CodiSmile design system styling), and *Accessibility* (high-contrast text and patient-friendly terminology).
5. **Reliability.** Measures the system's ability to maintain a specified level of operational performance. This includes *Maturity* (thoroughly debugged codebase verified through automated API testing), *Availability* (continuous system uptime throughout clinic operating hours), *Fault Tolerance* (graceful fallback mechanisms, such as deterministic mock inference when model weights are being updated), and *Recoverability* (automated scheduled database backups using `backup_db.py`).
6. **Security.** Ensures that clinical and patient personal data are protected against unauthorized disclosure or tampering. This includes *Confidentiality* (bcrypt password hashing complying with the 72-byte limit, JWT bearer token authentication separating staff and patient scopes, and authenticated image endpoints preventing public exposure), *Integrity* (relational constraints and audit logging), *Non-repudiation and Accountability* (append-only audit trail capturing administrative and clinical actions), *Authenticity* (strict session and role validation), and *Compliance* with the Philippine Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173).
7. **Maintainability.** Reflects the ease with which the software can be modified, enhanced, or adapted. This comprises *Modularity* (strict three-tier architecture separating React, FastAPI, PyTorch ML models, and PostgreSQL), *Reusability* (modular UI components and shared schemas), *Analyzability* (detailed server diagnostics and `/api/health` endpoint), *Modifiability* (independent retraining and swapping of YOLOv12 and KNN models without rewriting API logic), and *Testability* (automated pytest test suites and `evaluate_models.py` benchmarking).
8. **Portability.** Evaluates the ease with which Toothwise can be transferred across different deployment environments. This encompasses *Adaptability* (cross-browser responsiveness across Chrome, Firefox, and Edge), *Installability* (straightforward virtual environment and database deployment on clinic hardware), and *Replaceability* (modular configuration files enabling seamless migration to cloud or hybrid infrastructures).

# **1.4 Scope and Limitation of the Study**

The scope of this project covers the development, training, and deployment of an AI-based dental screening system at CodiSmile Dental Clinic. Using live video feeds and still images from a standard intraoral camera, the system will attempt to identify early signs of dental caries and common periodontal anomalies during patient consultations.   
The YOLOv12 model will be trained on publicly available annotated dental image datasets that cover healthy teeth, carious lesions, and signs of gum inflammation. Once training is complete, the system will be tested at CodiSmile Dental Clinic to see how it performs in an actual clinical environment. Aside from detection, the system will also generate a risk score and a personalized prevention plan for each patient based on what the model finds.  
   
There are, however, things this system cannot do. It is a support tool , not a replacement for a licensed dentist. The dentist at CodiSmile Dental Clinic will always have the final say on any diagnosis or treatment decision. The prevention plan it generates is meant to guide the patient, not serve as a formal medical prescription. The system also works only with intraoral camera images and does not process X rays or any other radiographic input. It will not detect oral cancer, bone loss, impacted teeth, or orthodontic issues, those remain outside the scope of what visual surface level detection can reliably identify.

# **1.5 Significance of the Study**

   
This study is expected to be useful to different groups of people in different ways.   
Patients. For patients of CodiSmile Dental Clinic, the main benefit is getting a faster and more thorough screening experience. Dental problems that might have been missed during a quick manual check can now be flagged by the AI. Getting a clear prevention plan at the end of the visit also gives patients something concrete to act on, which can make a real difference in their long-term oral health.

   
       	Dentists and CodiSmile Dental Clinic. The system helps dentists work smarter. Rather than spending a lot of time on routine visual checks, they can rely on the AI to do the initial screening and then focus their attention on the cases that actually need it. It also improves documentation since every detection result is recorded in the system automatically. 

       Future Researchers. Students and researchers who want to explore AI in dentistry can use this project as a starting point. The methodology, dataset approach, and system architecture are all things that can be built on or adapted for more advanced future studies.  
   
      The Research Community. There are very few local studies that apply AI to dental screening in the Philippine setting. This project adds to that small but growing body of work and can serve as a reference for similar initiatives in other clinics across the country.

**1.6 Definition of Terms**

   
         Artificial Intelligence (AI). A branch of computer science that focuses on building systems capable of performing tasks that would normally require human thinking, such as identifying objects in images or generating recommendations based on data.  
   
 	Computer Vision. A field within AI that deals with teaching machines to interpret and make sense of visual data, things like photographs or live video feeds.  
   
 	Deep Learning. A type of machine learning that uses layered neural networks to process complex patterns. In this project, deep learning is what allows the system to distinguish between healthy teeth, cavities, and inflamed gums in an image.  
   
 	Dental Caries  The clinical term for cavities or tooth decay. It happens when bacteria in the mouth produce acid that gradually eats away at the tooth's enamel and deeper layers.  
   
 	Flagging. When the system draws a bounding box around a part of the image where it has detected a potential dental anomaly, along with a label identifying what it thinks it found.  
   
 	Intraoral Camera. A small, handheld camera built to fit inside a patient's mouth. It takes high-resolution images or videos of the teeth and gums that are much clearer than what a dentist can see with the naked eye alone.  
   
 	Periodontal Anomalies. Problems that affect the gums and the structures that hold teeth in place. Common signs include redness, swelling, bleeding, or early signs of infection.  
   
 	Risk Categorization. The process of assigning a patient to a risk level , Low, Moderate, or High, based on what the AI detected during the screening and how confident it was in those detections.  
   
ISO/IEC 25010. An internationally recognized standard for Systems and Software Quality Requirements and Evaluation (SQuaRE) that categorizes software product quality into eight distinct characteristics: Functional Suitability, Performance Efficiency, Compatibility, Usability, Reliability, Security, Maintainability, and Portability. In this study, it provides the foundational evaluation framework for verifying the technical robustness and user acceptability of the Toothwise system.

YOLOv12 (You Only Look Once Version 12). The detection model used in this project. Introduced by Tian et al. (2025), it is known for being fast enough to work in real time while still being accurate enough for complex multi class detection tasks like identifying dental anomalies in a live camera feed.

**CHAPTER II**  
**REVIEW OF RELATED LITERATURE AND SYSTEMS**

This chapter presents the related literature and studies that have been gathered by the proponents. It introduces many ideas linked to the topic, which includes the research's principal focus. The study's synthesis is offered to analyze the previous research that the researchers have gathered.  
 

**2.1 Related Literature**

**Convolutional Neural Networks for Dental Image Diagnostics.** Schwendicke et al. (2021) put together a systematic review of how convolutional neural networks had been applied in dental imaging, covering everything from caries detection to tooth segmentation. What stood out from their findings was that CNN models were not just competitive with experienced dental clinicians but actually outperformed them in some cases. The authors were careful to point out, though, that the quality of training data matters enormously. Models trained on poorly labeled or inconsistent datasets tend to underperform in real clinical scenarios. They also made it clear that these tools are meant to assist dentists, not replace them. That design principle carries directly into Toothwise, where all detected cavity findings at CodiSmile Dental Clinic are reviewed by a licensed dentist before being communicated to any patient. The review also noted the absence of systems that go beyond detection and actually provide clinical guidance afterward, which is precisely the gap that the personalized prevention plan feature of Toothwise was built to address.

**Deep Learning for Caries Detection: A Systematic Review.** Mohammad Rahimi et al. (2022) reviewed a large number of studies that used machine learning and deep learning to detect caries across different image types, including intraoral photographs. Their main takeaway was that deep learning, particularly convolutional neural networks, worked reliably for identifying both early and more advanced carious lesions. They also raised a concern that is very relevant to this project: there are not many large, standardized, and publicly available dental datasets out there, which makes it harder to train models that perform well across different clinical settings. For Toothwise, this limitation was addressed by combining publicly available annotated datasets with data augmentation techniques during model training. The review also found that no existing study had combined automated caries detection with a recommendation output, which reinforces why the prevention plan feature of Toothwise fills a genuine gap in the existing body of work.

**Caries Detection with Tooth Surface Segmentation on Intraoral Images Using Deep Learning.** Park et al. (2022) took a two-step approach to detecting caries from intraoral photos by first segmenting individual tooth surfaces before running lesion detection on each one separately. By isolating the teeth before looking for cavities, the model produced fewer false positives compared to methods that ran detection on the full image without any preprocessing. More importantly for this study, the research confirmed that photos taken with intraoral cameras are detailed enough to support reliable artificial intelligence-based detection. That finding directly validates the image input approach used in Toothwise, where intraoral camera images serve as the primary data source for the YOLOv12 model during patient screenings at CodiSmile Dental Clinic.

**Detecting Dental Caries on Oral Photographs Using Artificial Intelligence.** Moharrami et al. (2024) focused specifically on artificial intelligence systems that detect caries from oral and intraoral photographs, which is the exact kind of image that Toothwise works with. Their review covered 19 studies from multiple countries and found that AI models applied to photographic inputs performed consistently well, especially for cavitated lesions that are clearly visible on the tooth surface. Most significantly, the authors explicitly identified the lack of systems that couple detection with actionable clinical recommendations as a gap that future research needs to address. This is the most direct identification in existing literature of the gap that Toothwise fills. The system does not stop at detection. It generates condition-specific dental health guidance for both the dentist and the patient through the integrated recommendation feature.

**Oral Health Philippines Country Profile.** The World Health Organization (2022) released a country-specific oral health profile for the Philippines as part of its Global Oral Health Status Report. The numbers are difficult to ignore. Dental caries was listed as one of the most prevalent health concerns in the country, with high rates of untreated cases across all age groups. The report also pointed out something that many Filipinos already know from experience: access to dental care is not evenly distributed. People in rural and community settings have significantly fewer options, and the limited dental workforce makes it harder to reach those who need care the most. This profile is the most authoritative reference for understanding the national oral health landscape that Toothwise seeks to contribute to. Deploying an artificial intelligence-assisted screening system at CodiSmile Dental Clinic is a concrete step toward addressing the access and consistency gaps that the WHO profile describes.

**Pediatrician Knowledge, Attitude and Practices on Children's Oral Health in the Philippines.** Oliveros Villarico et al. (2023) looked at something that often goes undiscussed, which is the role of pediatricians in preventing dental caries among Filipino children. Their study, conducted at a tertiary public hospital in Metro Manila, found that a significant number of pediatricians had limited awareness of evidence-based caries prevention approaches, even though the 2018 DOH National Survey on Oral Health already documented that 85.2% of Filipino five-year-olds had dental caries. The gap between what the data shows and what frontline healthcare workers actually know about it is striking. For this project, this literature helps explain why a tool like Toothwise matters at the clinic level. If even pediatricians are not fully equipped to address oral caries early, having an AI-assisted screening system that flags cavities during a regular consultation at CodiSmile Dental Clinic can make a real difference in catching problems before they get worse.

**Cost-Effectiveness Analysis of Oral Health Care Package of Services Under PhilHealth.** A 2025 health technology assessment published in collaboration with the Department of Health and PhilHealth found that approximately 29 million Filipinos have untreated dental caries, and that investing in early stage dental care at the primary level is actually more cost effective in the long run than dealing with advanced, untreated disease later. The economic argument is straightforward. Catching a cavity early costs far less than treating a severely decayed tooth that now requires extraction or restoration. This literature frames the financial case for why a tool like Toothwise is worth building. Catching cavities early is not just better for patients in terms of comfort and health outcomes. It is also the smarter approach from a public health spending perspective.

**Guiding Responsible Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare in the Philippines.** Alibudbud et al. (2025) wrote a narrative review and policy analysis on responsible AI adoption in Philippine healthcare. They went through the current landscape of AI applications in the country, examined what regulatory frameworks exist, and laid out recommendations for making sure AI tools in clinical settings are used ethically and safely. Some of the key concerns they raised were limited digital infrastructure, the lack of local clinical validation standards, and the need for healthcare workers to understand and critically evaluate AI outputs. They also emphasized that AI systems used in Philippine healthcare should be transparent, subject to human oversight, and compliant with the Data Privacy Act of 2012\. Reading this study shaped several decisions in how Toothwise was designed, particularly the requirement that all AI detection results at CodiSmile Dental Clinic must be reviewed and confirmed by a licensed dentist before they are communicated to patients, and that all patient data is stored securely in a locally managed database.

**2.2 Related Studies**

**Detecting White Spot Lesions on Dental Photography Using Deep Learning.** Askar et al. (2021) worked on detecting white spot lesions in intraoral dental photos using deep learning. White spot lesions are early stage demineralization, essentially the very beginning of a cavity before it becomes a visible hole. What made this study particularly useful is that it was done with a small dataset, which is a realistic constraint for many research projects, including this one. Despite that limitation, the model still managed to detect subtle surface level changes that would be easy to miss in a routine visual check. For Toothwise, this matters because it shows that even with limited annotated data, deep learning can pick up early, crucial changes from photographs, which is the same image modality the system uses at CodiSmile Dental Clinic. It also gave the team confidence that training a YOLOv12 model for early cavity detection is achievable even when the training dataset is not massive.

**Ultralytics YOLO (Version 8.0.0).** Jocher et al. (2023) released YOLOv8 as an open source framework under the Ultralytics platform. Compared to older YOLO versions, YOLOv8 came with a cleaner training pipeline, an anchor free detection head, and support for multiple tasks like detection, segmentation, and classification all in one package. It became one of the most widely used detection frameworks in both academic and applied settings because it was relatively easy to work with while still delivering strong results. Understanding YOLOv8 matters for this project because YOLOv12 was built on the same foundation. The training tools, dataset formats, and evaluation methods used in YOLOv8 largely carry over to YOLOv12, so much of what Jocher et al. (2023) established applies directly to how the Toothwise model was trained and tested.

**Diagnostic Accuracy of Dental Caries Detection Using Ensemble Deep Learning with Intraoral Camera Images.** Kang et al. (2024) took a different approach from most dental AI studies by using an ensemble of deep learning models rather than a single model for caries detection. By combining multiple detectors, they were able to reduce false positives while keeping sensitivity high, which is especially important in a clinical setting where unnecessary alarms can make dentists lose trust in the system. Their work was done using actual intraoral camera images from a real dental practice, not just radiographs, which makes it closely comparable to what Toothwise is doing. The models were validated against annotations made by experienced dentists, and the results held up well. This study gave the team confidence that deep learning for real-time intraoral caries detection is not just theoretically possible but has already been shown to work in a clinical environment similar to CodiSmile Dental Clinic.

**AI-Assisted Detection of Interproximal, Occlusal, and Secondary Caries on Bite-Wing Radiographs Using YOLOv8.** Karakus et al. (2024) applied YOLOv8 to the task of detecting different types of dental caries from bitewing radiographs. One thing that stood out in their findings was how well YOLOv8 handled small and overlapping lesions, which is a tricky problem in dental imaging because caries can be close together or partially hidden. Even though Toothwise uses intraoral photographs rather than radiographs, the core detection challenge is similar. The model needs to find and correctly label multiple small, curious areas within a single image. The performance of YOLOv8 in this study, combined with the architectural improvements introduced in YOLOv12, provided the team with a strong technical basis for believing that YOLOv12 can handle the cavity detection demands of Toothwise.

**YOLOv12: Attention-Centric Real-Time Object Detectors.** Tian et al. (2025) introduced YOLOv12 in a preprint that gained significant attention in the computer vision community. The paper presents a new approach to the YOLO architecture centered around area attention mechanisms, which allow the model to focus on relevant regions of an image rather than processing everything equally. The results were impressive. The YOLOv12 N configuration achieved 40.6% mean average precision at an inference latency of just 1.64 milliseconds on a T4 GPU, outperforming comparable YOLOv10 and YOLOv11 models. For a system like Toothwise that needs to run in real time during a dental consultation, that combination of accuracy and speed is exactly what is needed. This paper is the primary technical reference for the detection model used in this project, and its findings directly justify choosing YOLOv12 over earlier versions for deployment at CodiSmile Dental Clinic. It is also worth noting that no existing study has applied YOLOv12 to dental cavity detection, making Toothwise the first to explore this architecture in an intraoral dental screening context.

**Bridging the Gap: A Call for Capacity Building in AI for Healthcare in the Philippines.** A study from the University of Santo Tomas (2023) took a critical look at AI readiness in Philippine healthcare. When the researchers tested AI generated responses to clinical queries relevant to Filipino patients, they found notable inaccuracies, including instances where the AI produced fabricated references and incorrect medical guidance. The paper used this to argue that Filipino healthcare professionals urgently need better AI literacy and that unsupervised use of AI clinical tools carries real risks. The call to action was for structured training and, most importantly, mandatory human oversight in any clinical AI application. This study speaks directly to a design decision in Toothwise. The system does not allow AI detection results to be shown to patients without going through a dentist first. At CodiSmile Dental Clinic, the dentist reviews every output before it becomes part of the clinical record or is communicated to the patient, which is exactly the kind of human oversight that the UST study argued for.

**Synthesis**

The literature and studies reviewed in this chapter come together to build a clear and well-supported case for the approach that Toothwise has taken. Schwendicke et al. (2021) and Mohammad Rahimi et al. (2022) established through separate systematic reviews that deep learning models are genuinely reliable for dental caries detection, often performing at the level of trained clinicians or better. Park et al. (2022) and Kang et al. (2024) both confirmed that intraoral photographs are a sufficient and practical input modality for AI-based cavity detection, which directly validates the image acquisition approach of Toothwise at CodiSmile Dental Clinic.

The most important gap identified across the reviewed works was stated most directly by Moharrami et al. (2024): existing dental AI systems detect cavities but stop there. None of the systems reviewed generated recommendations or patient facing guidance after detection. Toothwise fills this gap by embedding a structured recommendation engine into the detection pipeline, making it the first system to pair YOLOv12-based cavity detection with an actionable personalized prevention plan.

On the technical side, Tian et al. (2025) established YOLOv12 as the most accurate and fastest real-time object detection model currently available, while Jocher et al. (2023) and Karakus et al. (2024) documented the strong performance of YOLO family architectures in dental detection tasks. Askar et al. (2021) further showed that deep learning cavity detection is achievable even under limited dataset conditions, supporting the training strategy used in this project.

The Philippine context literature from the WHO (2022), Oliveros Villarico et al. (2023), and the PhilHealth cost-effectiveness analysis (2025) grounds all of this in a concrete public health reality. Dental caries is widespread among Filipinos, it often go undetected until it has already progressed, and access to professional dental care remains out of reach for many due to cost and geography. Alibudbud et al. (2025) and the UST (2023) study shaped responsible design decisions around human oversight, data privacy, and clinical transparency. What no existing work has done is bring together YOLOv12-based real-time cavity detection, a personalized prevention plan generator, and a full-stack clinical system deployed at an actual Philippine dental clinic. That is the specific contribution of Toothwise.

**CHAPTER III**  
**METHODOLOGY**

This chapter presents the methodology used in the development of Toothwise: Teeth Cavity Detection with Recommendation System using YOLOv12 for CodiSmile Dental Clinic. It describes the development methodology, the composition and responsibilities of the four-member development team, the project planning and requirements analysis process, the major system design diagrams required for the capstone examination, and the development, testing, and screenshot documentation of the current system.

**3.1 Development Methodology**

Toothwise was developed using the Agile Software Development Life Cycle (Agile SDLC). Agile was selected because the system integrates several interconnected components, including a React.js web interface, a FastAPI REST backend, a PostgreSQL database, a dual-model YOLOv8/YOLOv12 detection pipeline, a KNN-based recommendation engine, authentication and authorization, audit logging, and a separate patient self-service portal. These components benefit from incremental development, continuous testing, regular review, and repeated refinement rather than a single sequential build.

Instead of completing the entire system in one long development cycle, the project was carried out through manageable iterations in which requirements were prioritized, features were implemented, tested, reviewed, and improved before the next set of features was developed. Each iteration followed the same general cycle of planning, requirements analysis, system design, development, testing, evaluation, and refinement, illustrated in Figure 1\.

**Figure 1 Agile Development Methodology**

The cycle in Figure 1 was applied repeatedly across the project's documented iterations. Planning and requirements analysis identified the features required for the clinic workflow; system design translated those requirements into frontend routes, API endpoints, and database structures; development implemented the corresponding React, FastAPI, and machine-learning components; testing verified the implemented behavior; evaluation compared the result against the intended requirements; and refinement corrected any issues found before the next iteration began.

**3.2 Project Planning**

The Toothwise project was planned around the screening and record-keeping workflow of CodiSmile Dental Clinic. The following considerations guided the planning of the system:

•  Project Objectives — to provide CodiSmile Dental Clinic with an AI-assisted dental screening system that detects possible cavities and related findings from an intraoral image, estimates a risk level, and generates a recommendation/prevention plan, while also supporting day-to-day clinic record-keeping.

•  Project Scope — the system covers staff authentication, patient management, dental screening and AI detection, risk assessment, recommendation generation, clinical notes, PDF reporting, audit logging, and a self-service patient portal.

•  Target Users — dentists and administrators at CodiSmile Dental Clinic, and the clinic's patients through the patient portal.

•  Clinic Workflow — a patient is registered or already on file, an intraoral image is captured or uploaded during a screening, the system produces detection, risk, and recommendation results for the dentist to review, and the dentist may add clinical notes or generate a PDF report.

•  Functional Requirements — detailed in Section 3.4.

•  Non-Functional Requirements — detailed in Section 3.4, covering security, usability, reliability, performance, and data protection.

•  AI Screening Requirements — the system was planned to use two independent detection models (YOLOv8 and YOLOv12) whose outputs are fused into a single clinical detection set, rather than relying on a single model.

•  Database Requirements — a relational PostgreSQL schema was planned to store dentists, patients, screenings, detections, recommendations, clinical notes, and audit logs with referential integrity between related records.

•  Security Requirements — JWT-based authentication, hashed passwords, rate-limited login endpoints, authenticated (non-public) image access, and audit logging were planned from the outset given the clinical and personal nature of the data involved. 

The requirements and technical decisions behind this planning were drawn directly from the current Toothwise project package rather than from separate interview transcripts or survey forms, since the project does not maintain those as separate dated records. Table 3.1 summarizes the actual sources used.

| **Database and schema review** | The PostgreSQL schema and migration scripts were reviewed to verify entities, relationships, enumerated values, detection sets, and audit logs. |
| **Testing and debugging records** | CHANGES.md documents API contract reconciliation, enum and image-path fixes, smoke testing, security validation, and feature verification. |
| **AI evaluation procedure** | The evaluate\_models.py utility defines how precision, recall, F1, mAP50, mAP50-95, and average inference time can be obtained from a labeled test set. No real model comparison values are claimed here since the current package documents the use of mock inference until trained weights are installed. |

**3.4 Requirements Analysis**

The requirements of Toothwise were analyzed from the intended clinic workflow and the functions represented in the current system and its API. Toothwise has two authenticated user groups: clinic-side users (dentists and administrators) and patients using the self-service portal. Tables 3.3 and 3.4 present the functional and non-functional requirements that are currently implemented in the application and verified against the project source code.

**Table 3 Functional Requirements**

| ID | Requirement | Specification |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **FR-01** | Staff authentication | Authenticate dentists and administrators by email and password and issue a JWT bearer token for authenticated API access. |
| **FR-02** | Role-based access | Distinguish administrator, dentist, and patient access scopes and restrict protected functions accordingly. |
| **FR-03** | Patient management | Create, view, update, and delete patient records and view screening history and risk trends. |
| **FR-04** | Dental screening | Submit an intraoral image in a single multipart screening request and receive detection, risk, recommendation, and screening-record results. |
| **FR-05** | AI detection | Run the configured YOLOv8 and YOLOv12 detectors, retain raw model outputs, and produce a fused clinical detection set. |
| **FR-06** | Risk assessment | Calculate a 0-100 risk score and classify the screening as LOW, MEDIUM, or HIGH. |
| **FR-07** | Recommendation generation | Use the KNN recommender and condition-specific rules to generate an ordered prevention plan. |
| **FR-08** | Screening review | View screening images, fused detections, risk information, recommendations, clinical notes, and model-comparison information. |
| **FR-09** | PDF report | Generate an authenticated PDF screening report containing patient/screening information, findings, prevention plan, and clinical notes. |
| **FR-10** | Patient portal | Patients register, log in, and view their own screening history and screening details. |
| **FR-11** | Audit logging | Record relevant authentication and create/update/delete actions for administrative review. |
| **FR-12** | Health monitoring | Expose a health endpoint that checks database connectivity without exposing internal errors. |
| **FR-13** | Database backup | Provide a pg\_dump-based backup utility that creates timestamped, retained backups. |

**Table 4 Non-Functional Requirements**

| ID | Quality Area | Specification |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **NFR-01** | Security | Passwords hashed with bcrypt; protected operations require JWT authentication; login/registration endpoints rate-limited to 5 requests per minute per IP. |
| **NFR-02** | Privacy | Screening images are not publicly exposed; authenticated and ownership-checked image endpoints are used instead of a public upload route. |
| **NFR-03** | Usability | Browser-based workflows for dashboard monitoring, patient records, screening, dentist management, audit review, and patient self-service. |
| **NFR-04** | Reliability | Backend returns a generic response for unhandled errors while recording diagnostic detail server-side. |
| **NFR-05** | Performance | YOLOv8 and YOLOv12 inference times are recorded per screening; model-comparison views report runtime and detection statistics. |
| **NFR-06** | Data Protection | Relational constraints, enumerated status/risk values, foreign keys, and transactions preserve consistent, valid records. |

***Data Flow Diagram Level 0***

Figure 4 presents the Level 0 (context) Data Flow Diagram of Toothwise, constructed in strict accordance with **Gane and Sarson notation rules**. Under Gane and Sarson conventions, the system boundary is modeled as a single central process (Process 0.0) rendered as a rounded rectangle divided into an upper process identifier section and a lower descriptive body. The three external entities—**System Administrator**, **Licensed Dentist / Clinical Staff**, and **Patient**—are represented as double-bordered and shaded rectangular source/sink symbols. All data exchanges are modeled using directed, labeled data flow arrows bearing specific noun phrases, ensuring that no direct entity-to-entity data flows occur without passing through the central system process.

![Figure 4 Toothwise Level 0 Data Flow Diagram (Context Diagram) — Gane and Sarson Notation](dfd_level_0_context_diagram.png)

**Figure 4 Toothwise Level 0 Data Flow Diagram (Context Diagram) — Gane and Sarson Notation**

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Dentist["LICENSED DENTIST / CLINICAL STAFF<br/>(CodiSmile Dental Clinic)"]
    Admin["SYSTEM ADMINISTRATOR"]
    Patient["PATIENT<br/>(Self-Service Portal)"]
    Toothwise(("0.0<br/>TOOTHWISE SYSTEM<br/>AI Dental Screening & Recommendation"))

    Dentist -->|"1. Staff Credentials<br/>2. Patient Profile & Vitals<br/>3. Intraoral Dental Image / Capture<br/>4. Clinical Notes & Override<br/>5. PDF Report Request"| Toothwise
    Toothwise -->|"1. Auth JWT Token<br/>2. Patient Records & History<br/>3. YOLOv8/v12 Detection Overlays<br/>4. Risk Score & Level (Low/Med/High)<br/>5. KNN Personalized Prevention Plan<br/>6. Authenticated PDF Screening Report"| Dentist

    Admin -->|"1. Admin Credentials<br/>2. Staff Account & Role Configuration<br/>3. Audit Log Filter Queries<br/>4. Database Backup Trigger"| Toothwise
    Toothwise -->|"1. Admin JWT Token<br/>2. Staff Roster & Profiles<br/>3. Tamper-Evident Audit Trail Logs<br/>4. System Health & Backup Status"| Admin

    Patient -->|"1. Portal Registration / Login Data<br/>2. Personal Screening Inquiry<br/>3. Dental Assistant Inquiries"| Toothwise
    Toothwise -->|"1. Patient JWT Token<br/>2. Personal Screening Findings & Badges<br/>3. Prevention Plan Recommendations<br/>4. AI Chatbot Guidance"| Patient
```

As modeled above, the Toothwise system acts as a centralized intelligent service. Clinical staff securely transmit patient vitals and intraoral imagery, receiving enriched detection bounding boxes, algorithmic risk tiers, and structured prevention plans in return. Administrative personnel supervise system integrity through dedicated audit logs and backup routines, while patients review their diagnostic history and personalized advice through authenticated portal channels. - **Capstone Project 1 (1st Semester: September 1, 2025 – December 19, 2025 | Weeks 1–17):** Focused on project initiation, clinical requirements analysis with CodiSmile Dental Clinic, architectural modeling (**Gane and Sarson DFDs**, ERD, and Use Case specifications), UI/UX wireframing, PostgreSQL schema initialization, core FastAPI backend setup (Iteration 1), and preliminary YOLOv8/v12 model training and feasibility evaluation, culminating in **Milestone 1** (Proposal Defense, October 2025) and **Milestone 2** (Midterm Architecture & Prototype Walkthrough, December 2025).

- **Capstone Project 2 (2nd Semester: January 5, 2026 – April 15, 2026 | Weeks 18–33):** Covered the full implementation of the dual-model AI detection pipeline and ensemble fusion (Iteration 2), the auditable 0–100 risk calculation engine and KNN recommendation system (Iteration 3), complete clinical workflow integration with live intraoral camera capture, ReportLab PDF generation, and the patient self-service portal (Iteration 4), extensive security hardening and automated TestClient verification (Iteration 5), clinical pilot deployment at CodiSmile Dental Clinic, and rigorous multi-stakeholder software quality evaluation based on the **ISO/IEC 25010 Product Quality Model**, concluding with **Milestone 3** (Pre-Oral Defense, March 2026) and **Milestone 4** (Final Oral Defense and System Turnover, April 15, 2026).

The Gantt chart in Figure 6 visualizes this same sequence.

The system was implemented as a three-tier web application: a React.js single-page frontend, a FastAPI REST backend exposing versioned JSON endpoints, and a PostgreSQL relational database. The AI detection pipeline (YOLOv8 and YOLOv12) and the KNN recommendation engine were developed as backend modules invoked synchronously by the screening endpoint. The complete technical specification of this architecture is presented in Chapter IV.

**3.7 System Testing**

Toothwise was tested through functional, integration, and security testing conducted against the running backend using FastAPI's TestClient, supplemented by manual and code-review verification for checks that are not easily exercised through an automated client alone. Table 3.8 presents the test cases executed against the current system and their documented results.

**Table 3.8 Toothwise Comprehensive System Test Cases and Verification Results**

| Test ID | Module / Area | Test Scenario | Pre-conditions & Test Inputs | Expected Result | Actual Documented Result | Status |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **TC-01** | Authentication | Staff Login - Valid Credentials | Registered staff account; POST /api/auth/login with valid email and password. | HTTP 200 OK; returns valid JWT access token and user role profile. | Verified successful login and JWT bearer token issuance. | PASSED |
| **TC-02** | Authentication | Staff Login - Invalid Password | Registered staff account; POST /api/auth/login with invalid password. | HTTP 401 Unauthorized; generic error message without disclosing user existence. | Verified HTTP 401 generic invalid-credential response and audit logging. | PASSED |
| **TC-03** | Access Control | Role-Based Access Control (Dentist vs Admin) | Authenticated dentist session; attempt GET /api/dentists/ or /api/audit/. | HTTP 403 Forbidden; admin-only endpoints strictly blocked for dentist role. | Verified HTTP 403 response; dentist restricted to clinical workflows. | PASSED |
| **TC-04** | Staff Management | Admin Creates New Dentist Account | Authenticated admin session; POST /api/dentists/ with valid name, email, role, license. | HTTP 201 Created; dentist record persisted with bcrypt hashed password. | Verified dentist profile creation and persistence in PostgreSQL. | PASSED |
| **TC-05** | Patient Management | Register New Patient Record | Authenticated staff session; POST /api/patients/ with valid demographic vitals. | HTTP 201 Created; patient record stored with unique patient_id. | Verified patient profile correctly created and searchable. | PASSED |
| **TC-06** | Patient Management | Update Patient Contact and Address | Existing patient record; PUT /api/patients/{id} with modified phone and address. | HTTP 200 OK; patient details updated with timestamp refresh. | Verified patient profile updated and audit log event generated. | PASSED |
| **TC-07** | Patient Management | Patient Soft Deletion / Deactivation | Existing patient with screening records; DELETE /api/patients/{id}. | HTTP 200 OK; is_active set to false; clinical screening records preserved. | Verified referential integrity preserved; historical screenings intact. | PASSED |
| **TC-08** | Image Acquisition | Upload Intraoral JPEG Image | Valid patient_id; multipart POST /api/screenings/ with valid JPEG photo. | HTTP 201 Created; image saved to disk with unique hashed filename; screening created. | Verified image stored securely; dimensions and path recorded in DB. | PASSED |
| **TC-09** | File Security | Upload Spoofed Non-Image File | Malicious file with .jpg extension containing executable script or text. | HTTP 400 Bad Request; server rejects file via in-memory byte header inspection. | Verified rejection before disk write; server logs invalid image format. | PASSED |
| **TC-10** | File Security | Upload Oversized Image (>15 MB) | File size exceeding configured 15 MB limit. | HTTP 413 Request Entity Too Large; upload aborted. | Verified file size boundary strictly enforced. | PASSED |
| **TC-11** | AI Screening | Dual Model YOLO Inference Execution | Valid intraoral image submitted; backend invokes YOLOv8 and YOLOv12 models. | Both models execute independently; raw bounding boxes and class labels produced. | Verified concurrent execution; per-model inference latencies recorded. | PASSED |
| **TC-12** | AI Screening | Ensemble Detection Fusion Logic | Overlapping detections from YOLOv8 and YOLOv12 on same tooth lesion. | Fusion engine clusters boxes via IoU >= 0.5; outputs single fused detection. | Verified fused detection set correctly generated without double-counting. | PASSED |
| **TC-13** | AI Screening | Five-Class Taxonomy Validation | Screening image with caries, calculus, and gum inflammation. | Detections correctly mapped to taxonomy classes without hardcoded index mismatch. | Verified label taxonomy matches embedded weights and schema enums. | PASSED |
| **TC-14** | Performance | Model Runtime Telemetry Recording | End-to-end screening request processed. | Screening record stores exact yolov8_ms and yolov12_ms integer values. | Verified timing metrics stored and displayed in model comparison view. | PASSED |
| **TC-15** | Risk Assessment | Risk Score Computation Formula | Screening with 2 high-confidence caries findings and 1 gingivitis finding. | Confidence-weighted severity formula calculates 0-100 score + multi-finding bonus. | Verified risk score computed accurately according to auditable formula. | PASSED |
| **TC-16** | Risk Assessment | Risk Level Categorization Thresholds | Test cases with scores of 25 (Low), 50 (Medium), and 85 (High). | Scores <35 classified LOW; 35-69 classified MEDIUM; >=70 classified HIGH. | Verified risk_level enum accurately assigned across all threshold boundaries. | PASSED |
| **TC-17** | Recommendation | KNN Feature Vector Construction | Patient age = 28, detected caries count = 2, mean confidence = 0.88. | Engine builds standardized feature vector matching trained model dimensionality. | Verified feature vector correctly constructed by build_feature_vector(). | PASSED |
| **TC-18** | Recommendation | Personalized Prevention Plan Composition | Screening classified into HIGH risk tier with carious lesions. | Generates ordered recommendation items prioritizing urgent clinical care followed by hygiene. | Verified prevention plan contains condition-specific, prioritized advice. | PASSED |
| **TC-19** | Recommendation | Recommender Offline Artifact Loading | FastAPI startup initialization. | Recommender successfully loads knn_recommender.joblib artifact from disk. | Verified model loaded into memory with fallback to synthetic retrainer. | PASSED |
| **TC-20** | Clinical Workflow | Dentist Authors Clinical Notes | Authenticated dentist reviews screening; POST /api/screenings/{id}/notes. | HTTP 201 Created; note linked to screening and authoring dentist. | Verified clinical notes persisted and retrievable in screening details. | PASSED |
| **TC-21** | Clinical Workflow | Enforce Clinical Note Length Cap | Submission of clinical note exceeding maximum configured character limit. | HTTP 422 Unprocessable Entity; payload rejected. | Verified input validation prevents unbounded text injection. | PASSED |

| **TC-23** | Patient Portal | Patient Self-Service Portal Registration | Unregistered patient submits name, contact, email, and password. | HTTP 201 Created; patient account created with portal login credentials. | Verified patient registration and subsequent portal authentication. | PASSED |

Test cases T-08, T-09, T-10, T-12, T-13, and T-14 specifically verify the issues identified and corrected during the system's security hardening pass, described further in Section 4.8. Testing was performed against the mock detector where the trained model weights were not yet available; the procedure for evaluating real trained weights once available is described in Section 4.5.

In addition to automated unit, integration, and security test cases, the system was formally evaluated by key stakeholders in accordance with the ISO/IEC 25010 Software Product Quality Model. A standardized 5-point Likert scale evaluation questionnaire was administered to ten (10) respondents, comprising five (5) IT professionals / system analysts and five (5) dental healthcare practitioners (licensed dentists and clinic staff) from CodiSmile Dental Clinic. **CHAPTER IV**  
**TECHNICAL SPECIFICATIONS**

This chapter presents the current technical specifications of Toothwise: Teeth Cavity Detection with Recommendation System using YOLOv12 for CodiSmile Dental Clinic. The specifications reflect the implemented system contained in the current Toothwise v5 project package, including the React.js web frontend, FastAPI backend, PostgreSQL database, YOLOv8 and YOLOv12 detection pipeline, KNN recommendation engine, authentication, audit logging, reporting, and patient portal.

**4.1 Software Specifications**

**4.3 System Architecture**

Toothwise is organized as a three-tier web application with an integrated machine-learning pipeline, shown in Figure 4.1. The presentation tier is the React.js frontend, containing separate workflows for staff (dashboard, patients, patient details, screening capture, screening details, dentist management, and the admin-only audit log) and for patients (registration, login, viewing their own screening history, and asking the built-in screening assistant about their own results). The application tier is the FastAPI backend, which exposes REST endpoints under the /api prefix and coordinates authentication, patient operations, screening requests, risk scoring, recommendations, reports, and audit logging. The data tier is PostgreSQL. The YOLOv8/YOLOv12 detector and the KNN recommender operate as backend machine-learning modules invoked synchronously by the screening endpoint rather than as separate external services.

![][image15]

**Figure 1 Three-Tier Toothwise System Architecture**

Figure 4.2 shows the screening-specific processing flow: intraoral image capture or upload, image validation, parallel YOLOv8/YOLOv12 detection, detection fusion, risk scoring and recommendation generation, persistent storage, and presentation of the result to the dentist and, where applicable, the patient.

![][image16]

**Figure 2 Toothwise Screening Process Flow**

**4.4 Database Technical Specifications**

The Toothwise database is implemented in PostgreSQL 15 and defined in database/schema.sql. It contains seven tables—dentists, patients, screenings, detections, recommendations, clinical\_notes, and audit\_logs—related as shown earlier in the Entity Relationship Diagram (Figure 3.3). Enumerated types constrain dentist roles, patient sex, risk level, source model, detection set, and detection label to a fixed set of valid values. Tables 4.5 to 4.11 present the field-level specification of each table.

**Table 4.5. dentists table**

Stores staff accounts for administrators and dentists.

| Field | Type | Description |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **id** | SERIAL PK | Unique dentist/administrator identifier. |
| **last\_name** | VARCHAR | Staff member's last name (surname). |
| **middle\_name** | VARCHAR | Staff member's middle name or initial (nullable). |
| **first\_name** | VARCHAR | Staff member's first (given) name. |
| **email** | VARCHAR, UNIQUE | Login email; used for JWT authentication. |
| **hashed\_password** | VARCHAR | bcrypt password hash; plaintext is never stored. |
| **role** | ENUM (admin, dentist) | Determines access to admin-only functions (dentist management, audit log). |
| **license\_no** | VARCHAR, nullable | Dentist's professional license number. |
| **is\_active** | BOOLEAN | Enables disabling an account without deleting its history. |
| **created\_at** | TIMESTAMP | Record creation timestamp. |

**Table 4.6. patients table**

Stores patient records, including optional patient-portal login credentials.

| Field | Type | Description |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **id** | SERIAL PK | Unique patient identifier. |
| **last\_name** | VARCHAR | Patient's last name (surname). |
| **middle\_name** | VARCHAR | Patient's middle name or initial (nullable). |
| **first\_name** | VARCHAR | Patient's first (given) name. |
| **birthdate** | DATE, nullable | Used to compute age for risk/recommendation context. |
| **sex** | ENUM, nullable | Patient sex on file. |
| **contact\_number** | VARCHAR, nullable | PH mobile number on file for the patient. |
| **address** | VARCHAR, nullable | Patient address on file. |
| **email** | VARCHAR, UNIQUE, nullable | Patient-portal login email, where self-registered. |
| **hashed\_password** | VARCHAR, nullable | bcrypt hash for patient-portal login; null for staff-entered records without portal access. |
| **is\_active** | BOOLEAN | Enables disabling a portal account without deleting clinical history. |
| **created\_at** | TIMESTAMP | Record creation timestamp. |

**Table 4.7. screening table**

Stores one record per dental screening event.

| Field | Type | Description |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **id** | SERIAL PK | Unique screening identifier. |
| **patient\_id** | INTEGER, FK → patients.id | Owning patient. |
| **dentist\_id** | INTEGER, FK → dentists.id, nullable | Dentist who performed/reviewed the screening. |
| **image\_path** | VARCHAR | Server-side path to the stored intraoral image. |
| **image\_width / image\_height** | INTEGER | Stored image dimensions. |
| **risk\_level** | ENUM (low, medium, high) | Derived risk classification (Section 4.6). |
| **risk\_score** | INTEGER (0-100) | Underlying numeric risk score (Section 4.6). |
| **yolov8\_ms / yolov12\_ms** | INTEGER | Per-model inference time, used for model-comparison reporting. |
| **created\_at** | TIMESTAMP | Screening timestamp. |

**Table 4.8. detection table**

Stores individual bounding-box findings for a screening from both raw and fused detection sets.

| Field | Type | Description |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **id** | SERIAL PK | Unique detection identifier. |
| **screening\_id** | INTEGER, FK → screenings.id | Owning screening. |
| **label** | VARCHAR | Detected finding class (e.g., caries, gum\_inflammation). |
| **confidence** | FLOAT | Model confidence score for the detection. |
| **x1, y1, x2, y2** | FLOAT | Bounding box coordinates on the source image. |
| **source\_model** | ENUM (yolov8, yolov12, fused) | Which model produced this detection. |
| **detection\_set** | ENUM (fused, yolov8\_raw, yolov12\_raw) | Distinguishes the clinical fused set from each model's raw output, preventing the double/triple counting issue identified during development. |

**Table 4.9. recommendations table**

Stores the ordered prevention-plan items generated for a screening.

| Field | Type | Description |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **id** | SERIAL PK | Unique recommendation identifier. |
| **screening\_id** | INTEGER, FK → screenings.id | Owning screening. |
| **text** | VARCHAR | Recommendation text shown to the dentist/patient. |
| **priority** | INTEGER | Marks condition-specific/urgent items for visual emphasis. |
| **order\_index** | INTEGER | Preserves the intended display order of the prevention plan. |

Stores dentist-authored notes attached to a screening.

| Field | Type | Description |

| Field | Type | Description |

**4.5 AI/ML Technical Specifications**

Toothwise runs two independent object-detection models over the same intraoral image rather than relying on a single model. Each model runs through the pipeline shown earlier in Figure 4.2.

•  YOLOv8 and YOLOv12 Ensemble — the detector runs both models independently over the same intraoral image. Raw outputs are retained as yolov8\_raw and yolov12\_raw for per-model comparison, while the fused detection set is stored as fused and drives the clinical risk and recommendation workflow.

•  Model Comparison — the in-app model comparison view reports per-model runtime (yolov8\_ms, yolov12\_ms) and per-image agreement between the two detectors. This is a runtime/agreement comparison, not a ground-truth accuracy test, since a single unlabeled patient photo has no ground truth to score against.

•  Inference Mode — the current package defaults to a deterministic mock detector until trained yolov8\_dental.pt and yolov12\_dental.pt weight files are installed, allowing the rest of the system to be developed, tested, and demonstrated end-to-end independently of model training progress.

•  Label Taxonomy — the detector reads class names from each model's own embedded weights rather than a hardcoded list, so a model trained on fewer classes still integrates correctly; any class defined in the system's taxonomy but absent from a given model's training data simply cannot be produced by that model.

***4.5.1 Model Evaluation Procedure***

Real accuracy/precision/recall/mAP evaluation is performed once trained weights exist, using backend/training/evaluate\_models.py. The utility runs each YOLO model's own validation routine (model.val()) against a labeled test split and produces a comparison table of precision, recall, F1, mAP50, mAP50-95, and average inference time for both models. No such values are reported in this document, since the current package documents the use of mock inference until trained weights are installed; reporting fabricated accuracy figures here would misrepresent the system's actual, current evaluation status.

**4.6 Risk Assessment Technical Specifications**

The risk engine (backend/app/ml/risk\_engine.py) converts a screening's fused detections into a single risk score and level using a rule-based, auditable formula rather than a separate machine-learning model:

•  Score computation — the score is derived from the confidence-weighted maximum severity across the screening's findings, plus a small capped bonus added when multiple concerning findings are present, producing a score from 0 to 100\.

•  Level thresholds — a score below 35 is classified LOW, 35 to 69 is classified MEDIUM, and 70 or higher is classified HIGH. The risk\_level stored on the screening record is derived directly from this threshold, not computed separately.

•  Downstream use — risk\_level (not the raw score) drives the dashboard's high-risk case count, all risk badges shown in the interface, and the PDF report header. The raw numeric score is retained internally and used to plot the patient's risk-trend chart, but is not displayed to users as a bare number, since a rule-based heuristic score can otherwise appear more precise than it is.

**4.7 Recommendation Engine Technical Specifications**

The recommendation engine (backend/app/ml/recommender.py) is independent of the risk engine — it builds its own feature vector from the screening's raw detections and the patient's age, rather than consuming risk\_score.

•  Algorithm — a K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classifier with K=5, trained offline and persisted as an artifact (knn\_recommender.joblib) loaded by the backend at runtime.

•  Feature vector — built from the detection confidences/counts per finding class and the patient's age, as defined in build\_feature\_vector().

•  Output — the trained model classifies the screening into a risk tier, which is then used to compose an ordered prevention plan from condition-specific and general oral-health recommendation items (generate\_prevention\_plan()).

•  Training data — the current package includes a synthetic dataset generator (\_synthesize\_dataset()) used to train and validate the recommender pipeline prior to substitution with real clinical outcome data, and a retrain\_from\_real\_data() utility to retrain the model once such data is available.

**4.8 Security Technical Specifications**

Toothwise underwent a dedicated security-hardening pass documented in CHANGES.md. The current, verified security posture is as follows:

•  Authentication — JWT bearer tokens identify staff and patient scopes separately, using distinct token/session keys so a staff and a patient session can coexist in the same browser without colliding.

•  Password storage — passwords are hashed with bcrypt; plaintext passwords are never stored. Password length is explicitly validated against bcrypt's 72-byte limit rather than being silently truncated.

•  Rate limiting — login and registration endpoints are rate-limited to 5 requests per minute per IP address to reduce brute-force risk.

•  Image access control — patient dental photos are served only through authenticated, ownership-checked image endpoints; the previous public, unauthenticated static file mount was removed during hardening.

•  Upload validation — uploaded images are validated from their actual file bytes in memory before any disk write, rather than trusting a client-supplied content-type header.

•  Input validation — explicit length caps are enforced on free-text fields (clinical notes, addresses) to prevent unbounded input.

•  Authorization boundaries — patient-facing routes use ownership checks and do not trust a client-supplied patient\_id when accessing another patient's screening records.

•  Error handling — a global exception handler returns a generic response for unhandled errors without leaking internal detail, while still allowing legitimate 404/400 responses through.

•  Response headers — X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, and Permissions-Policy headers are set on API responses as a baseline security posture.

•  Audit logging — an append-only audit\_logs table records authentication events and sensitive create/update/delete actions for administrative review, accessible only to the admin role.

A remaining, explicitly documented tradeoff is that JWTs are stored in the browser's localStorage rather than an httpOnly cookie. This is a theoretical XSS-related token-theft risk; however, no exploitable XSS surface currently exists in the frontend (no dangerouslySetInnerHTML or eval usage was found in the codebase). Migrating to httpOnly cookies is documented as a future hardening item rather than treated as resolved.

**4.9 Network and Deployment Specifications**

The documented deployment model is a local-area-network configuration. A server machine hosts the FastAPI application, PostgreSQL database, and YOLO inference services. Authorized clinic workstations access the React.js interface through a modern browser using the server's local network address, as shown earlier in Figure 4.1. The patient portal uses the same application services but enforces a separate patient JWT scope and ownership checks. Screening images are not exposed through a public static-file route; authenticated image endpoints are used instead. Internet access is useful for development, dependency installation, and repository synchronization, but the documented local application workflow does not depend on an external cloud database.

Table 4.12 presents the step-by-step implementation procedure used to deploy Toothwise onto the clinic's local server and network.

**Table 4.12. Implementation / Deployment Procedure**

| Step | Procedure |
| :---- | :---- |
| **1\. Prepare the server** | Install Python 3.11, PostgreSQL 15+, Node.js 18+, Git, and the required system dependencies. Create the application directories and configure environment variables. |
| **2\. Prepare PostgreSQL** | Create the Toothwise database and apply database/schema.sql. For an existing database, apply the documented idempotent migration scripts in the required order when applicable. |
| **3\. Configure the backend** | Create and activate the Python virtual environment, install backend/requirements.txt, configure DATABASE\_URL, CORS origins, SECRET\_KEY, upload limits, model paths, and other environment variables. |
| **4\. Initialize application data** | Start the FastAPI backend so SQLAlchemy ensures the required tables exist. Run seed\_accounts.py when the documented seeded clinic accounts are required. |
| **5\. Configure AI models** | Place trained yolov8\_dental.pt and yolov12\_dental.pt files in backend/models\_weights/ and set USE\_MOCK\_MODEL=false when real model inference is ready. Until then, the configured mock detector supports end-to-end demonstration and integration testing. |
| **6\. Prepare the frontend** | Install Node.js dependencies with npm install, configure the frontend API base URL as required by the deployment environment, and run npm start for development or create a production build. |
| **7\. Connect the local network** | Connect the server and authorized clinic workstations to the same local network. Allow browser clients to reach the FastAPI service at the server's local address and configured API port. |
| **8\. Verify security and functions** | Test login, patient records, screening, report generation, audit logging, image access, and patient ownership boundaries before operational use. |
| **9\. Establish backups** | Use database/backup\_db.py with PostgreSQL pg\_dump to create timestamped compressed backups and retain the most recent fourteen backups. Schedule the utility through Windows Task Scheduler when required. |
| **10\. Operational transition** | Provide the clinic users with the system URL, account procedures, workflow guidance, and backup/maintenance instructions. Monitor the /api/health endpoint and review audit logs for administrative traceability. |

(A good summary should be comprehensive, concise, coherent, and independent. These qualities are explained below:

1. **A summary must be comprehensive.** You should isolate all the important points in the original passage and note them down in a list. Review all the ideas on your list, and include in your summary all the ones that are indispensable to the author’s development.  
2. **A summary must be concise.** Eliminate repetitions in your list, even if the findings restate the same points. Your summary should be considerably shorter than the source. You are hoping to create an overview; therefore, you need not include every repetitions of a point or every supporting detail.  
3. **A summary must be coherent.** It should make sense as a piece of writing in its own right; it should not merely be taken directly from your list of notes or sound like a disjointed collection of points.  
4. **A summary must be independent.** You are expected to maintain your own voice throughout the summary. Don’t simply quote other’s research works; Instead use your words to express your understanding of what you have read. After all, your summary is based on your interpretation of the findings points or ideas.
